title: Apple Rumored to Drop the iPhone's Action Button Next Year - MacRumors
summary: Apple plans to merge the iPhone's Action button with the Camera Control starting next year, according to the leaker known as "Instant Digital". In a new post on Weibo, the leaker claimed that a single press of the combined button would open the camera, while a long press would trigger the function assigned to the Action button. They explicitly clarified that the dedicated Action button would disappear, while the Camera Control button would remain.
text:
Apple plans to merge the iPhone's Action button with the Camera Control starting next year, according to the leaker known as " Instant Digital ."

In a new post on Weibo, the leaker claimed that a single press of the combined button would open the camera, while a long press would trigger the function assigned to the Action button. They explicitly clarified that the dedicated Action button would disappear, while the Camera Control button would remain.

The proposed arrangement seems plausible given how the two features already work. The Action button predates the Camera Control and requires a long press to activate its assigned function, while a single press of the Camera Control opens the camera. Combining them in the way described would therefore preserve both familiar interactions, with the customizable action simply moving to a different location on the device.

A long press of Camera Control currently opens Visual Intelligence , but that feature has since been integrated directly into the Camera app as Siri mode in iOS 27 . That integration could give Apple room to reassign the gesture while keeping Visual Intelligence accessible through the Camera app.

It is notable that the iPhone Duo also lacks an Action button , despite retaining Camera Control. Its omission provides a precedent for an iPhone without the separate control and could hint at a broader change in the future.

title: Valve escaped Windows. Now Steam is breaking free from the PC itself - PCWorld
summary: Steam Deck made Windows optional. Steam Frame takes aim at x86. Valve is building a future where your Steam library barely cares what kind of computer sits underneath it. Is that good for gamers?
text:
Valve spent the last decade making Windows optional for PC gaming . Now it wants to do the same thing to x86 — the Intel- and AMD-based CPU architecture at the heart of every gaming PC. If it succeeds, the resulting shake-up could change what “PC game” even means.

The Steam Deck proved Valve’s Proton compatibility layer could run an enormous library of Windows games on Linux without developers needing to port them to Linux first. That breakthrough helped make the Steam Deck a success. It also made Linux gaming legitimately viable, and laid the groundwork for SteamOS to spread to other PCs.

But the Steam Frame reveals that Valve’s ambitions go much deeper. The standalone VR headset runs SteamOS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor based on the Arm architecture, rather than the x86 processors from AMD and Intel that have powered PC gaming for decades.

And Valve expects your existing x86 Windows games to run on it anyway. That’s why the Arm chip inside Steam Frame matters so much more than VR. Valve is starting to dismantle the fundamental assumptions about which hardware and software a gaming PC needs to run your games.

The writing is on the wall. We’re looking at the endgame for everything Valve has been building with SteamOS, Proton, Steam Deck, and now Steam Frame: Buy anywhere, play anywhere. Your Steam library won’t care what operating system you’re using, what processor architecture sits inside your device, or, eventually, even what type of device you’re holding

title: OpenAI's new cyber model found ways to attack nearly 1000 Linux flaws - Axios
summary: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber will initially be available to a small number of approved customers due to concerns that, in the wrong hands, it could supercharge cyberattacks.
text:
OpenAI has debuted a new AI model geared towards helping cybersecurity professionals. The company says that the new model, called GPT-6 Cyber, outperforms its general-purpose GPT-6 Astra model on most cyber tasks. Because of the risk that the model could be used to conduct cyberattacks if it fell into the wrong hands, OpenAI is current making the model available only to a small handful approved security customers. Fortune first reported that OpenAI was planning to release a specialized cyber model based on GPT-6 in September.

As AI models have become better at finding software flaws and turning them into working attacks, businesses have come under increasing pressure to strengthen their cyber defenses. Gartner forecast in September that worldwide AI cybersecurity spending would reach $51.3 billion this year, nearly double last year’s $25.9 billion. OpenAI is increasingly leaning into this market, seeing it as an important path to growing its enterprise sales. This is OpenAI’s fourth cybersecurity-focused model this year, following versions released in April, June and August. The company also hired a chief revenue officer, Dali Rajic , who comes from a cybersecurity software background.

title: Is The Xbox Series X More Powerful Than The Steam Machine? - BGR
summary: Gamers have eagerly anticipated Valve's console for years. Despite using newer parts, though, it's pretty evenly matched against an Xbox.
text:
vfhnb12/Shutterstock Add BGR on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover The console wars rage on as Valve's latest device, the Steam Machine, joins the competition. Microsoft launched the Xbox Series Xin 2020. The Steam Machine launched in June 2026 allowing users to play PC games on a TV and monitor instead of strictly on a PC. Both systems can play the latest AAA release, but only one is technically more powerful.

Valve's console costs $1,049 for the base version, but it's a mighty machine with a semi-custom 6-core / 12-thread AMD Zen 4 and an AMD RDNA 3 GPU sporting 28 CUs. That's much newer hardware than the Xbox Series X's custom AMD Zen 2 CPU and AMD RDNA 2 GPU with 52 CUs. As a result, the Steam Machine is more efficient with newer processing capabilities, including better support for AI through FSR upscaling. However, in terms of performance, the Xbox Series X boasts more than 12 TFLOPS, while the Steam Machine is estimated to reach nearly 9 TFLOPS. The Xbox also features 16GB of GDDR6 RAM, whereas Valve's Steam machine uses 16GB of RAM and 8GB of GDDR6 VRAM for graphics.

What that all adds up to is a surprisingly even match, with specialized features making any difference. The Steam Machine, without a controller, is still nearly $300 more than the Xbox Series X's $800 price-tag, controller included. If you want to play games without paying a high price, there are powerful gaming systems that cost much less than a Steam Machine.
